units.title: The Sense Organs
units.intro:
Receptors turn a stimulus into a nerve impulse. Skin: touch, pressure, pain, temperature. Nose: chemoreceptors in the air stream. Tongue: taste buds (sweet, salt, sour, bitter — umami may be named). Eye: cornea + lens focus on the retina; rods = dim/black-white; cones = colour in bright light; iris controls pupil. Ear: pinna → canal → drum → ossicles → cochlea (hearing) and semicircular canals (balance).

Internal receptors watch stretch, blood chemistry, posture — they feed homeostasis in Grade 11.

cards.title: More detail — eye and ear
body: Eye path: cornea does most of the bending, lens does the fine focus (accommodation: fat lens for near, thin for far). Iris circular and radial muscles set pupil size. Blind spot = optic nerve exit, no receptors. Short sight: long eyeball, image in front of retina, diverging lens. Long sight: short eyeball or stiff lens, converging lens.

Ear path: air waves → drum → three bones amplify → oval window → fluid in cochlea → hair cells → auditory nerve. Semicircular canals detect rotation (fluid lag). Eustachian tube equalises pressure with the throat.

cards.title: 7.1.1 The Skin
body: **The skin** is the sense organ which covers the whole body.
For example the fingertips, lips and cheeks have the greatest concentration of receptors and are, therefore, more sensitive to their respective stimuli.
Skin receptors receive a signal and transmit it via nerve cells to the brain.
In the brain, the signals are interpreted as sensations.

cards.title: 7.1.2 The Nose
body: The nasal cavity is lined with mucous membranes that have smell receptors, which are connected to the olfactory nerve.
The smell itself consists of vapours of various substances.
The smell receptors are sensitive to different types of sensations and interact with the molecules of various vapours, transmitting the sensations to the brain through the olfactory bulb.
The chemical molecules of any odorous substance that enter the nose dissolve in the mucus and stimulate the olfactory receptors.

cards.title: 7.1.3 The Tongue
body: **The tongue** is a sense organ that helps identify taste.
The human tongue is dotted with thousands of taste buds, which are made up of many receptor cells.
Many of the taste buds are found in large swellings, called papillae.
Generally, the taste buds close to the tip of the tongue are sensitive to sweet tastes, whereas those at the back respond to bitter tastes.

cards.title: 7.1.4 The Eye
body: Human eyes are situated in the eye sockets of the skull.
The sockets give protection to the eyes.
A number of muscles hold the eyes in place, enabling them to move in different directions.
The front of the eyeball is covered by a thin, transparent membrane, the conjunctiva.

cards.title: 7.1.5 The Ear
body: **The ear** is the sense organ that assists in hearing.
The external ear: The external ear consists of the pinna, auditory canal and eardrum (tympanum).
The pinna helps to direct sound waves into the auditory canal.
Glands in the walls of the auditory canal produce a waxy material.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following structures acts as a thin, protective membrane covering the front of the eyeball and lining the eyelids?

steps.text: **Given:** Anatomical structures covering the anterior surface of the eye.

**Concepts:** The conjunctiva is a thin, transparent mucous membrane that covers the front of the eyeball (except the cornea) and lines the inner surface of the eyelids, providing protection and lubrication.
The cornea is transparent but is a structural layer focusing light.
The sclera is the white, tough outer coat.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What is the primary function of the Eustachian tube in the human ear?

steps.text: **Given:** Anatomical structures of the middle ear.
**Concepts:** The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity to the pharynx, allowing air to pass in and out to equalize pressure across the eardrum.
Sound amplification is done by the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes).
Equalization of pressure prevents the eardrum from rupturing or dampening vibrations, which is mediated by the Eustachian tube.

cards.answer: Equalization of air pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In bright light conditions, which of the following pupillary muscular actions occurs?

options.A: Radial muscles contract, dilating the pupil
options.B: Circular muscles contract, constricting the pupil
options.C: Radial muscles relax, constricting the pupil
options.D: Circular muscles relax, dilating the pupil

cards.why:
**Given:** Pupillary response to high light intensity.

**Concepts:** The iris contains antagonistic muscles. In bright light, parasympathetic stimulation causes the circular (sphincter) muscles to contract, reducing pupil diameter to limit light entry.

**Steps:**
1. Bright light requires pupillary constriction.
2. Constriction is executed by the contraction of circular muscles.
3. Dilation (in dim light) is executed by the contraction of radial muscles.

**Final Result:** **Circular muscles contract, constricting the pupil** is the correct anatomical reflex.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which area of the retina lacks rod cells entirely, consists exclusively of cone cells, and serves as the point of maximum visual acuity?
cards.why:
**Given:** Visual acuity regions of the retina.

**Concepts:** The fovea centralis (yellow spot) contains a high density of cone photoreceptors and no rod cells, making it the center of sharpest vision.

**Steps:**
1. The blind spot (optic disc) lacks both rods and cones where axons exit.
2. The fovea is located at the center of the retina and contains only cones.
3. Highly concentrated cones facilitate maximal resolution.

**Final Result:** **Fovea Centralis (Yellow Spot)** is the site of maximum visual acuity.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Constriction and dilation of the eye pupil is associated with the
cards.why: The **iris** is the colored part of the eye. It contains circular and radial muscles that control the size of the **pupil**. By constricting (getting smaller) or dilating (getting larger), the iris regulates the amount of light entering the eye.

cards.title: 7.2 The Internal Receptors
body: Receptors that receive information about internal body conditions are called **internal receptors**.
Organisms receive information about a stimulus or changes within their body with the help of these receptors.
Internal receptors detect stimuli related to muscle length and tension, limb position, pain, blood composition, blood volume, blood pressure, body temperature, etc.
Internal receptors can be classified as mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors and chemoreceptors.
Mechanoreceptors are specialized receptors that monitor pressure, stretching, and bending forces.

cards.title: Explain how internal receptors keep the body informed
cards.problem: A person stands up quickly and feels dizzy for a moment, then recovers. Explain the role of internal receptors.

steps.text: **Step 1: Name the change.** Standing quickly lowers blood pressure in the head for a moment.
**Step 2: Name the receptors.** Pressure receptors (baroreceptors – a kind of mechanoreceptor) in the aorta and carotid arteries detect the fall.
**Step 3: Message.** They send impulses to the brain (medulla).
**Step 4: Response.** The brain raises the heart rate and narrows blood vessels, so blood pressure returns to normal and the dizziness passes.

cards.answer: Baroreceptors (internal mechanoreceptors) detect the drop in blood pressure and signal the brain, which raises heart rate and constricts vessels to restore pressure.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following structures acts as a thin, protective membrane covering the front of the eyeball and lining the eyelids?
cards.why:
**Given:** Anatomical structures covering the anterior surface of the eye.

**Concepts:** The conjunctiva is a thin, transparent mucous membrane that covers the front of the eyeball (except the cornea) and lines the inner surface of the eyelids, providing protection and lubrication.

**Steps:**
1. The cornea is transparent but is a structural layer focusing light.
2. The sclera is the white, tough outer coat.
3. The conjunctiva is the superficial mucous membrane that protects the cornea from friction.

**Final Result:** **Conjunctiva** is the correct structure.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary function of the Eustachian tube in the human ear?

options.B: Equalization of air pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane
options.C: Transmission of neural impulses to the auditory cortex
options.D: Maintenance of dynamic and static bodily equilibrium

cards.why:
**Given:** Anatomical structures of the middle ear.

**Concepts:** The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity to the pharynx, allowing air to pass in and out to equalize pressure across the eardrum.

**Steps:**
1. Sound amplification is done by the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes).
2. Equalization of pressure prevents the eardrum from rupturing or dampening vibrations, which is mediated by the Eustachian tube.
3. Neural transmission is done by the auditory nerve.

**Final Result:** **Equalization of air pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane** is the primary function.

tips.text: Humans are equipped with internal and external receptors that help them respond to changes in their body and the environment. These receptors are very important in the survival of the organism.
Some of the receptors form sense organs like the skin, nose, tongue, eye and ear. These sense organs respond to different stimuli in the environment.
The sense organs and stimuli they respond to are listed below.
Receptors which recognize different sensations, like pain, touch, pressure, etc. are present in the skin.
The nose is the sense organ where olfactory receptors are present.
Receptors, which recognize the primary tastes such as sweet, sour, bitter and salty, are present in the tongue.
The eye is the sense organ that helps us to see objects in our surroundings.
Images in the eye are formed on the retina, where rod and cone cells (the photoreceptors) are located.
The structures of the human ear assist in hearing sound.
The malfunctioning and non-functioning of sense organs are hazardous to one’s health. Therefore, we should take precautions for their care and proper functioning.

questions.q: A patient at an eye clinic in Asmara has a healthy retina whose rods and cones generate nerve impulses normally, but those impulses are not being interpreted as images. According to the table in the unit, in which part of the brain are impulses from the eye normally interpreted?
why: **Identify the sense organ and its receptors.** The eye is the photoreceptive organ described in the unit; its rods and cones convert light into nerve impulses that must be carried to the brain for interpretation.

**Use the unit's sense-organ table.** The table pairs each sense organ with its interpreting brain region: Skin - Somatosensory Cortex, Nose - Olfactory Bulb/Temporal Lobe, Tongue - Gustatory Cortex, Eye - Occipital Lobe, Ear - Temporal Lobe (Auditory)/Cerebellum.

**Check every distractor.** The temporal lobe interprets auditory (and olfactory) input, the somatosensory cortex interprets touch, pressure, temperature and pain from the skin, and the gustatory cortex interprets impulses from the taste buds. None of these interprets visual impulses, so each is a pairing error for a different sense organ.
**Conclude.** Only the occipital lobe is given as the region for interpreting impulses from the eye, so option A is the single correct choice.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A student in Keren burns her tongue on hot tea and then tastes the sugar dissolved in it. According to the unit's sense-organ table, in which brain region are impulses from the taste buds of the tongue interpreted? A) Gustatory cortex  B) Occipital lobe  C) Olfactory bulb  D) Somatosensory cortex
why: **Identify the receptors firing.** The taste buds on the papillae of the tongue are chemoreceptors; they detect sweet, sour, salty and bitter chemicals dissolved in saliva.
**Match the organ to the brain region.** The unit's table pairs the Tongue (Chemoreceptors/Taste Buds) with the Gustatory Cortex.
**Reject the distractors.** The occipital lobe serves the eye, the olfactory bulb serves the nose, and the somatosensory cortex serves the skin, so none of them interprets taste.

questions.q: A farmer near Nakfa picks up a smooth, cool stone. According to the unit's sense-organ table, which brain region interprets the impulses coming from the mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors of his skin? A) Somatosensory cortex  B) Occipital lobe  C) Gustatory cortex  D) Olfactory bulb

**Match the organ to the brain region.** The table lists the Skin (Mechanoreceptors, Thermoreceptors) with the Somatosensory Cortex.
**Reject the distractors.** The occipital lobe interprets light, the gustatory cortex interprets taste and the olfactory bulb interprets smell, so they cannot interpret skin sensations.

questions.q: The unit states that one human retina contains about $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and about $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells. During a laboratory lesson at a secondary school in Asmara, a student must compare the two populations. Calculate the ratio of rod cells to cone cells and express it in the form $$n : 1$$.
questions.answer: rod cells : cone cells = $$20 : 1$$ (there are 20 times as many rod cells as cone cells)
why: **Identify the two quantities.** Number of rod cells = $$1.2 \times 10^8$$; number of cone cells = $$6.0 \times 10^6$$, both for a single retina.
**Write the ratio.** rod cells : cone cells = $$1.2 \times 10^8 : 6.0 \times 10^6$$.

**Make the powers of ten equal.** Convert the cone count to the same power of ten as the rod count: $$6.0 \times 10^6 = 0.060 \times 10^8$$, so the ratio becomes $$1.2 \times 10^8 : 0.060 \times 10^8$$.

**Divide both parts by the cone value.** The common factor $$10^8$$ cancels, leaving $$1.2 : 0.060$$. Dividing both numbers by 0.060 gives $$1.2 \div 0.060 = 120 \div 6 = 20$$ and $$0.060 \div 0.060 = 1$$.
**State the ratio.** rod cells : cone cells = $$20 : 1$$, meaning there are 20 times as many rod cells as cone cells in the retina.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: The unit gives about $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and about $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells in one retina. A health club in Massawa wants the comparison written as the number of cone cells present for every 100 rod cells. Calculate this number.
questions.answer: 5 cone cells for every 100 rod cells
why: **Set up the comparison.** cones per 100 rods = $$\dfrac{6.0 \times 10^6}{1.2 \times 10^8} \times 100$$.
**Scale to 100 rods.** $$0.05 \times 100 = 5$$, so there are 5 cone cells for every 100 rod cells.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: The unit gives about $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and about $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells per retina. In a biology notebook kept at a school in Nakfa, a student wants the totals for both retinas of one person. Calculate the total number of rod cells and the total number of cone cells in both retinas.
why: **Recognise that there are two retinas.** The unit's figures are for one retina, so each population must be multiplied by 2 for a person with two eyes.
**Double the rod cells.** $$2 \times 1.2 \times 10^8 = 2.4 \times 10^8$$ rod cells.
**Double the cone cells.** $$2 \times 6.0 \times 10^6 = 12 \times 10^6 = 1.2 \times 10^7$$ cone cells.

questions.q: Complete each blank with the correct term from the unit. (a) Baroreceptors located in the ______ and the ______ constantly measure the stretch of blood-vessel walls in order to monitor blood pressure. (b) Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect the partial pressures of ______ and ______ as well as the pH of arterial blood. (c) Proprioceptors are specialized mechanoreceptors found in muscles, ______ and ______ which give the brain continuous feedback about body position and muscle length.
questions.answer: (a) carotid sinuses and aortic arch; (b) oxygen ($$\text{O}_2$$) and carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$); (c) tendons and joints
why: **Recall the baroreceptor locations.** The unit states that baroreceptors are located in the carotid sinuses and the aortic arch, where they constantly measure the stretch of blood-vessel walls to monitor blood pressure.

**Recall what peripheral chemoreceptors detect.** Carotid and aortic bodies contain peripheral chemoreceptors that detect the partial pressures of oxygen ($$\text{O}_2$$) and carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$) as well as pH levels in arterial blood.
**Recall the proprioceptor locations.** Proprioceptors are specialized mechanoreceptors located in muscles, tendons and joints, providing feedback about body position, muscle length and joint angles.
**Assemble the completed statements.** (a) carotid sinuses and aortic arch; (b) oxygen and carbon dioxide; (c) tendons and joints.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Complete each blank with the correct term from the unit. The internal thermoreceptors that act as the body's central thermostat are located in the ______ of the brain, and they directly monitor the temperature of the ______ flowing through the brain. When the core temperature rises, this centre triggers ______ of cutaneous blood vessels and ______ production.
why: **Locate the central thermostat.** The unit states that thermoreceptors within the hypothalamus of the brain act as the body's central thermostat, monitoring the temperature of the blood flowing through the brain.
**Recall the response to a rise in core temperature.** A rise above the optimal $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ triggers vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels and sweat production.
**Assemble the completed statement.** hypothalamus; blood; vasodilation; sweat.

questions.q: Complete each blank with the correct term from the unit. Stretch receptors in the ______ prevent over-inflation, while stretch receptors in the ______ signal the autonomic nervous system when a critical volume of fluid has been reached. Both belong to the internal receptor group called ______.
why: **Recall the internal stretch receptors.** The unit states that stretch receptors in the lungs prevent over-inflation, while those in the bladder signal the autonomic nervous system when a critical volume of fluid is reached.
**Classify the receptor group.** Stretch receptors respond to mechanical deformation, so they are mechanoreceptors - one of the three functional groups of internal receptors.
**Assemble the completed statement.** lungs; bladder; mechanoreceptors.

questions.q: A Grade 10 class in Keren is preparing an eye-health leaflet using the unit's figures for one retina: about $$1.2 \times 10^8$$ rod cells and about $$6.0 \times 10^6$$ cone cells. (a) Calculate the total number of photoreceptor cells in the two retinas of one person. (b) Calculate the percentage of this total that is made up of cone cells, giving your answer to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) $$2.52 \times 10^8$$ photoreceptor cells in both retinas; (b) cone cells make up about 4.8% of the total
why: **Find the photoreceptors in one retina.** Total in one retina = rod cells + cone cells = $$1.2 \times 10^8 + 6.0 \times 10^6$$. Writing the cone count with the same power of ten, $$6.0 \times 10^6 = 0.060 \times 10^8$$, gives $$(1.2 + 0.060) \times 10^8 = 1.26 \times 10^8$$ photoreceptors.
**Double it for two retinas.** $$2 \times 1.26 \times 10^8 = 2.52 \times 10^8$$ photoreceptor cells in both retinas (252,000,000 cells).
**Find the cone cells in two retinas.** $$2 \times 6.0 \times 10^6 = 1.2 \times 10^7$$ cone cells.
**Write the percentage relationship.** Percentage of cones = $$\dfrac{\text{cone cells}}{\text{total photoreceptors}} \times 100 = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^7}{2.52 \times 10^8} \times 100$$.
**Carry out the division.** $$\dfrac{1.2 \times 10^7}{2.52 \times 10^8} = \dfrac{1.2}{25.2} = 0.047619\ldots$$
**Convert to a percentage and round.** $$0.047619 \times 100 = 4.7619\%$$, which rounds to 4.8% to one decimal place.

questions.q: A dockworker at the port of Massawa spends two hours working in very hot conditions and his core temperature rises above normal. Explain how the internal thermoreceptors of the hypothalamus detect this change and how the body brings the core temperature back towards $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$. Name the two corrective responses described in the unit and state whether this control loop is negative feedback.
questions.answer: The hypothalamus thermoreceptors detect core blood temperature above $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ and trigger (i) vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels and (ii) sweat production; both responses remove heat and lower the core temperature back towards the optimum. A fall below $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ would instead trigger vasoconstriction and shivering. The loop is negative feedback because the response reverses the initial change and restores homeostasis.
why: **Identify the internal receptor and what it monitors.** Internal thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus act as the body's central thermostat. They do not monitor the outside air; they directly monitor the temperature of the blood flowing through the brain.

**Compare the detected value with the optimum.** The unit gives the optimal core temperature as $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$. Working in the heat at Massawa pushes the core blood temperature above this set value, so the thermoreceptors increase their signalling to the hypothalamus.

**Corrective response 1: vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels.** The hypothalamus triggers vasodilation of cutaneous blood vessels, so a larger volume of warm blood flows close to the skin surface and heat is lost from the body to the surroundings.
**Corrective response 2: sweat production.** The hypothalamus also triggers sweat production. Evaporation of sweat from the skin surface removes heat from the body and lowers the core temperature.

**State the opposite arm of the same control system.** The same centre works in reverse: if the core temperature fell below $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$, the hypothalamus would trigger vasoconstriction of cutaneous blood vessels and shivering in order to conserve and generate heat.

**Identify the type of feedback.** The responses reverse the original deviation - a rise in core temperature is answered by heat-losing mechanisms - so the loop is negative feedback, and it returns the internal state to the narrow survival range (homeostasis).

questions.q: A student from Asmara goes camping in the highlands on a cold night and his core temperature begins to fall below $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$. Explain how the internal thermoreceptors respond, name the two corrective responses described in the unit, and state the type of feedback involved.
questions.answer: The hypothalamic thermoreceptors detect core blood temperature below $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ and the hypothalamus triggers (i) vasoconstriction of cutaneous blood vessels to conserve heat and (ii) shivering to generate heat. This is negative feedback because the responses reverse the original fall in temperature and restore the optimum.
why: **Detect the deviation.** The internal thermoreceptors of the hypothalamus continuously monitor the temperature of the blood flowing through the brain; a value below the optimal $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$ is the stimulus.
**Response 1: conserve heat.** The hypothalamus triggers vasoconstriction of cutaneous blood vessels, reducing blood flow near the skin surface so that less heat is lost to the cold surroundings.
**Response 2: generate heat.** Shivering is triggered, and the muscular activity generates heat that raises the core temperature.
**Classify the loop.** Both responses oppose the initial change, so the mechanism is negative feedback that brings the core temperature back towards $$37\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$$.

questions.q: A runner at a stadium in Asmara sprints while holding his breath as long as he can, so carbon dioxide accumulates in his arterial blood. Using the unit's description of internal receptors, explain how this change is detected and how the body responds, naming the receptor groups involved.
questions.answer: Rising carbon dioxide makes the blood more acidic. Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect the raised $$\text{CO}_2$$ partial pressure and lowered pH of arterial blood, while central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata monitor the pH of the cerebrospinal fluid. Together they trigger an immediate reflex to increase ventilation, expelling the excess carbon dioxide and restoring blood pH.
why: **Identify the chemical change.** Holding the breath allows carbon dioxide to accumulate, and the unit states that a rise in $$\text{CO}_2$$ leads to blood acidity (a fall in pH).

**Peripheral detection.** The carotid and aortic bodies contain peripheral chemoreceptors that detect partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide as well as pH levels in arterial blood, so they detect the acidic blood.
**Central detection.** Central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata monitor the pH of cerebrospinal fluid and serve as the primary controller of the respiratory drive.

**The corrective response.** These chemoreceptors trigger an immediate reflex to increase ventilation, so excess carbon dioxide is expelled and blood pH is restored - another negative feedback loop that maintains homeostasis.
